answer: Yes: the submit handler is the shared helper srv/handlers/transition.js built with transition('O', 'S'), which reads the order's status_code and rejects with 409 unless it equals 'O', so the server enforces "status_code = O" for Orders.submit. The parser missed it because the handler is a require()'d factory result (handler module -> transition helper); this require-a-factory pattern recurs for all three actions and is a candidate for a deterministic rule.

findings.title: Orders.submit enforces status_code = O in the transition helper
findings.statement: srv/order-service.js registers the submit handler from srv/handlers/submit.js, which exports transition('O', 'S'). The transition step selects the order's status_code and calls req.reject(409) when it is not 'O', then updates it to 'S'. The UI's Core.OperationAvailable rule (status_code = O) is therefore backed by a server check in the Node handler, not only hidden in the UI. Only the OrderService action path is covered: AdminService exposes sales.Orders without this handler, so an Admin could still write status_code directly.

evidence.quote: if (order.status_code !== from) return req.reject(409, `Only orders in status ${from} can do this`)
module.exports = (from, to) => function (req) { return step(this.entities.Orders, req, from, to) }

findings.test: POST /orders/Orders(ID=aaaaaaaa-0000-0000-0000-000000000002,IsActiveEntity=true)/OrderService.submit as alice (order not in status O) should return 409 "Only orders in status O can do this".
